code.title: CommonJS vs ESM: copies, require anywhere, no this

followUps: Node looks at the file extension first, then the nearest package.json, then (newer versions) the code itself. .mjs is always ESM and .cjs is always CJS. For a plain .js file, Node walks up to the closest package.json and reads "type": "module" means ESM, "commonjs" or missing means CJS. If the type is missing and the file contains import/export or top-level await, recent Node versions detect the syntax and run it as ESM. Being explicit with "type" is the safest choice.

The dual package hazard is when one package ships both an ESM and a CJS build and an app ends up loading both copies. Each copy has its own module state, so you get two singletons, two caches, and instanceof checks that fail between objects made by different copies. Example: a Logger class created by require('lib') in one file is not an instanceof the Logger from import 'lib' in another. Fixes: ship ESM only, or keep all state in a CJS core that a thin ESM wrapper re-exports.

In modern Node (20.11+ and 22) use import.meta.dirname and import.meta.filename. In older versions, derive them from import.meta.url:

import { fileURLToPath } from 'node:url';
import path from 'node:path';
const __filename = fileURLToPath(import.meta.url);
const __dirname = path.dirname(__filename);

The URL is a file:///... string, so you must convert it to a path rather than slicing the text.

code.title: Live binding vs copied value

followUps: Because function declarations are hoisted with their body, while const bindings are hoisted only as an uninitialized slot. When module A and B import each other, one of them runs first. A function declaration is fully usable from the start of its module's setup, so the other side can call it even before the code runs. A const f = () => {} sits in the temporal dead zone until its line executes, so reading it early throws ReferenceError. Calling it later, after both modules finished, is fine.

A bundler renames each module's top-level variables into one shared scope, so an import becomes a direct reference to the exporter's variable, with no copy. Example: export let count becomes a variable count$1 in the bundle, and the importer's count is rewritten to count$1, so updates are visible. When it cannot concatenate (for example code-split chunks), it keeps a namespace object with getters such as get count() { return count$1; }, which also reads the current value each time.

code.title: Iterator protocol and early exit with return()

followUps: Because array destructuring uses the iterator protocol and stops early, so it calls return() on the iterator when it has taken what it needs. With const [a] = gen() only one value is requested; the iterator is not finished, so the engine closes it, which runs the generator's finally blocks. If the pattern ends with a rest ([a, ...rest]), the iterator is drained instead and done becomes true, so no return() is needed. This is why a generator holding a file handle is released even when you only read its first item.

An async iterable has a [Symbol.asyncIterator]() method whose iterator's next() returns a Promise of { value, done }. for await (const x of src) awaits each result before running the body, so one item is handled at a time. It also works on ordinary iterables (awaiting each value). Async generators (async function*) implement it for you:

async function* g() { yield 1; yield 2; }
for await (const v of g()) console.log(v);

Breaking out calls return() for cleanup, like for...of.

Iterator helpers are methods on Iterator.prototype (ES2025): map, filter, take, drop, flatMap, reduce, toArray. They are lazy because each returns a new iterator that does work only when asked for the next value. Example: naturals().filter(n => n % 2).map(n => n * n).take(3).toArray() pulls just enough items to produce three results and never builds a huge intermediate array, so it also works on infinite sources.

code.title: Generators: next(value), throw(), return()

followUps:
yield* hands control to another iterable, passing its values through one by one, and the whole expression evaluates to the return value of the inner generator (the value of its final done: true result). Values sent with next(x) and errors from throw() are forwarded to the inner one too.

function* inner() { yield 1; return 'end'; }
function* outer() { const r = yield* inner(); yield r; }
// yields 1, then 'end'

For plain arrays or strings it evaluates to undefined.

Write a driver that runs the generator and treats every yielded value as a promise: wait for it, then resume the generator with the result (or throw the error into it).

function run(genFn) {
  const it = genFn();
  const step = (m, v) => { const r = it[m](v);
    return r.done ? r.value : Promise.resolve(r.value).then(x => step('next', x), e => step('throw', e)); };
  return Promise.resolve().then(() => step('next'));
}

yield plays the role of await. This is how the co library worked before async/await existed.

A generator has to save and restore its state (locals, position) on each resume and allocate a result object { value, done } per step, while a plain loop just runs in registers. Engines optimise this well, but it is often several times slower for tight loops. Example: summing 10 million numbers through for...of on a generator may take noticeably longer than an indexed for. It matters only in hot paths with millions of items; for normal code, readability and laziness (never building a big array) are usually worth more than the overhead, so measure before changing it.

code.title: Map vs object and Set vs array

followUps:
Use JSON.stringify on an array of entries, because JSON.stringify(map) alone gives {}. Convert out and back:

const m = new Map([['a', 1], ['b', 2]]);
const json = JSON.stringify([...m]); // [["a",1],["b",2]]
const back = new Map(JSON.parse(json));

If all keys are strings you can use Object.fromEntries(m) instead. Non-string keys (objects) cannot survive JSON, and nested Maps need the same treatment, for example with a replacer function that turns Maps into entry arrays.

Because a Set compares values with SameValueZero, and objects (arrays included) are equal only if they are the same reference. The two literals [1,2] are two separate arrays in memory, so the Set keeps both and size is 2. A Set with const a = [1,2]; new Set([a, a]) has size 1. To deduplicate by content, build a key such as JSON.stringify(arr) or arr.join(',') and keep a Set of those strings.

V8 stores Maps and Sets as ordered hash tables (a deterministic hash table). Entries live in an array in insertion order, and a separate bucket array maps a hash to the chain of entries. Lookup is average O(1), and iteration just walks the entry array, which gives insertion order for free. Deleting marks the slot as removed, and the table is rebuilt when it fills up or has too many holes. Running iterators survive resizing because the table keeps a link to its replacement.

code.title: WeakMap for private per-object data

followUps:
A WeakRef is a pointer to an object that does not keep it alive; a WeakMap key is also weak but you must already have the key to look anything up. deref() returns the object while it exists, and undefined once the garbage collector has reclaimed it, which can happen at any time after the object becomes otherwise unreachable. So you must always handle the empty case:

const o = ref.deref();
if (o) use(o); else rebuild();

Within one synchronous run of code, deref() on the same ref gives a consistent answer.

FinalizationRegistry lets you register a callback that may run after an object is garbage collected, for example to free an external handle. You should never rely on it because the engine gives no guarantee about when, or even whether, the callback runs (a program may exit first, and engines may delay it). Use it only as a safety net or for cache cleanup, never for correctness like closing files or releasing locks. For those, use explicit cleanup: try/finally, using with Symbol.dispose, or a close() method.

Yes, and it is fine: a WeakMap value that references its own key does not keep the key alive. WeakMap entries are ephemerons: the value is kept alive only if the key is reachable from somewhere else. So wm.set(obj, { owner: obj }) forms a cycle that the collector understands, and when nothing else references obj, both the key and the value are freed together. A plain Map would leak here because the Map itself holds the key strongly.

code.title: Map cache that never shrinks, and an LRU fix

followUps: Closures capture the variables of the scope they were created in, so a listener that mentions a big object keeps that whole object alive for as long as the listener is registered. Example: a handler on a long-lived window or event emitter uses el inside, so removing el from the page does not free it, because the emitter holds the handler and the handler holds el. Fix by removing the listener on unmount (removeEventListener or an AbortController signal), or by not capturing large objects.

Create an object, hold it only through a WeakRef, drop the strong reference, force a collection, and assert the ref is empty. Run with node --expose-gc:

let el = makeComponent(); mount(el); unmount(el);
const ref = new WeakRef(el); el = null;
await new Promise(r => setTimeout(r, 0));
global.gc();
assert.equal(ref.deref(), undefined);

If the cache still retains it, deref() returns the object and the test fails. Wait a tick first, since the engine can keep a ref alive until the current job ends.

code.title: Symbols as keys and well-known symbols

followUps: Because string conversion of a Symbol is blocked on purpose: the language treats implicit conversion as a likely mistake, so `${Symbol('x')}` and 'a' + sym throw TypeError. String(sym) is an explicit request, so it is allowed and returns "Symbol(x)"; sym.description returns just "x". This prevents silently turning a unique key into an ordinary string that could collide with other keys.

using x = getResource(); declares a block-scoped constant and, when the block ends (normally or by an exception), automatically calls x[Symbol.dispose](). Resources are disposed in reverse order of declaration. await using does the same with Symbol.asyncDispose and awaits it.

{
  using f = { [Symbol.dispose]() { console.log('closed'); } };
  console.log('working');
} // prints working, then closed

It is like try/finally written once on the object instead of at every use.

code.title: Proxy with Reflect: validation, negative index

followUps:
Proxy invariants are rules the engine enforces so a trap cannot lie about facts the target makes permanent. For example, if the target has a non-writable, non-configurable property x = 1, the get trap must return 1; returning anything else throws TypeError.

const t = {};
Object.defineProperty(t, 'x', { value: 1 });
new Proxy(t, { get: () => 2 }).x; // TypeError

Similarly, ownKeys must include all non-configurable keys, and a frozen target cannot report a property as missing.

Map and Set methods, and #private fields, work on internal slots that only the real object has; a proxy has none. Calling proxy.get(k) runs Map.prototype.get with this set to the proxy, and it throws TypeError: incompatible receiver. The same happens for this.#x when this is a proxy. Fix by binding methods to the target in the get trap (typeof v === 'function' ? v.bind(target) : v), which is what Vue does with instrumented collection methods.

Proxies are noticeably slower than direct access: every get or set goes through your trap function and the engine cannot inline or optimise the property access as well. Typical overhead is several times slower per operation, which is irrelevant for config objects or form state, but hurts in hot loops over big data. Mitigations: proxy only what you need, avoid traps you do not use (a missing trap falls back to the fast default), cache nested proxies, and use Reflect for the default behaviour. Measure for your case.

code.title: Tiny reactive system with Proxy

followUps: Vue tracks iteration with the ownKeys trap, which for...in, Object.keys and spread all call. Inside ownKeys it calls track(target, ITERATE_KEY), a special key that stands for "the list of keys". When a property is added or deleted, set (for a new key) or deleteProperty calls trigger(target, ITERATE_KEY), so effects that looped over the keys re-run. Plain value changes to existing keys do not need this. For arrays the same idea uses length.

Signals avoid proxies by making each reactive value an explicit cell, such as const count = signal(0), read with count() or count.value and written with count.set(1). Reading inside an effect or computed subscribes it, as in the proxy design. Pros: no proxy overhead, fine-grained updates, nothing to break with Map/Set or #private, and it works with primitives. Cons: you must call the accessor, it is less seamless than plain objects, and nested data needs a signal per field or a store helper. Proxies read like normal JavaScript.

code.title: Optional chaining and ?? pitfalls

followUps: Because a?.b.c short-circuits the whole chain only when a itself is null or undefined; the ?. checks only the thing directly before it. If a exists but a.b is null, the expression continues to .c on null and throws TypeError. Example: with a = { b: null }, a?.b.c throws, while a?.b?.c gives undefined. Add ?. at every step that can really be missing, but no more.

TypeScript uses the truthiness check to remove undefined and null from the type inside the if. If user is User | undefined and profile is Profile | undefined, then inside if (user?.profile) both user and user.profile are narrowed to defined types, so user.profile.city compiles without another check. Note that a truthiness check also drops 0 or '' for those types; for a nullish-only check write user?.profile != null.

When ESM is loaded through require, Node returns the module namespace object. If the ESM has a default export, you reach it as .default. To let CJS callers get the default export directly, the ESM can add a named export called "module.exports" (spelled with a string export name): export { api as 'module.exports' };. Then require('lib') returns api itself instead of a namespace object. Without it, CJS users write require('lib').default, which surprises people.

Bundlers read CJS dependencies, wrap them in a small function so require and module.exports exist, and then expose the result to ESM imports. Vite pre-bundles dependencies with esbuild in dev for this reason, converting CJS to ESM and merging many small files into one. Named imports from CJS work through interop: the bundler treats module.exports as the default export and tries to guess the names. Because the exports are dynamic, tree-shaking is weak for CJS, so prefer packages that ship ESM.

Go in small safe steps. First, add tests and a lockfile, and update dependencies that already ship ESM. Then convert leaf files (those that import nothing local) to ESM, because CJS code can require(esm) on modern Node, so consumers do not break. Move inward, replacing __dirname with import.meta.dirname and require with import, one package at a time, committing each step. Set "type": "module" per package once its files are done. A codemod such as cjs-to-esm helps for the mechanical part, and you check with CI on every step.

code.title: Sync generator, async function and async generator

followUps: The return() method of the async generator runs, so its finally blocks execute and the source is closed. When for await exits early (break, return or an error), it calls iterator.return() and awaits it. If the generator is paused at a yield, execution resumes as if a return happened there, so cleanup such as closing a file or a connection runs. Example: with try { yield* rows } finally { await db.close(); }, breaking out after the first row still closes the database.

RxJS fits when many things can push values at you and you need to combine them. Observables are push-based and multicast: several subscribers can share one stream, and operators such as debounceTime, switchMap, merge and combineLatest handle time-based logic like search-as-you-type and cancelling stale requests. An async iterator is pull-based with one consumer, so it has no back-pressure problem but cannot natively merge two event sources or drop values. Use async iterators for sequential data, and RxJS for event streams.
